# Cellulose vs Fiberglass Blown In Insulation

If you’re weighing quotes for **cellulose vs fiberglass blown in insulation**, the material name alone won’t tell you which proposal is right for your San Antonio home. Ask how the installer will prepare the attic, achieve consistent coverage, address air leaks, and follow the exact product’s installation instructions. This **blown-in cellulose vs fiberglass** comparison focuses on those job details, because the performance of loose-fill insulation depends on the product and the assembly it goes into.

Geo-Insulation’s published blown-in service page says the company installs loose-fill fiberglass. It does not list cellulose installation. The guide below is a general way to compare proposals, not an assessment of your attic or a recommendation for a specific product.

## Start with the attic and the quote

Before comparing materials, make sure you understand what each bid includes. A quote should identify the insulation product, the areas to be covered, the intended installed depth or target, and any preparation or removal work. Ask whether the contractor will inspect existing insulation and look for conditions that should be addressed before adding more.

Insulation slows heat flow, but it does not by itself seal every air leak or correct a roof leak. The U.S. Department of Energy’s guidance on [adding blown insulation to existing attics](https://bsesc.energy.gov/energy-basics/blown-insulation-existing-attics) discusses preparing the attic and addressing air leakage before insulation is installed. That makes the assembly and the work plan important parts of a **loose-fill insulation comparison**, not just the material in the bags.

Useful questions for either bid include:

- Which exact product will you install, and can I review its installation instructions?
- What areas will be insulated, and how will you check that coverage is even?
- What existing insulation will remain, and what would prompt removal?
- Are air leaks or ventilation details included in the scope?
- How will the finished work be checked and documented?

A clear answer should explain what the contractor plans to do in your attic, rather than relying only on broad claims about a material.

## Coverage and installation quality

Loose-fill insulation is installed in place, where it can be distributed around framing and other attic features. But “blown in” does not automatically mean every area will be covered correctly. The installer needs to follow the product’s instructions and account for the shape and condition of the attic.

Ask how the crew will handle narrow areas, obstructions, and the edges of the insulated space. Also ask how they will avoid blocking ventilation paths or covering components that need to remain visible or accessible. The U.S. Department of Energy’s [guide to insulation types and installation](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-03/insulation_guide_0.pdf) explains that installation details matter and that loose-fill insulation can settle if it is not installed properly.

Compare proposals by the planned work and verification, not by a promise of “gap-free” coverage alone. A useful bid describes the areas included, the product-specific installation approach, and how the contractor will check the result.

## Settling: ask about the exact product

Avoid treating settling as a simple contest between cellulose and fiberglass. Products differ, and installation matters. Rather than relying on a general statement that one material never settles, request the manufacturer’s coverage information and installation instructions for the product named in the quote.

Ask the installer what installed depth and coverage the product instructions call for, and whether the proposal accounts for settling as specified by the manufacturer. If two bids use different products, compare their documentation and the scope of work side by side. A product-specific answer is more useful than a blanket claim about all insulation of one material type.

## Moisture: investigate the cause, not just the material

Neither cellulose nor fiberglass should be treated as a fix for a moisture problem. If the attic has a roof leak, damp insulation, water staining, or other signs of moisture, ask what caused it and whether it needs correction before new insulation is added. Covering a problem without addressing its source can leave the underlying condition unresolved.

The Department of Energy guidance on existing attic insulation recommends checking attic conditions as part of the work. If you see wet materials, damaged framing, or signs of mold, get a qualified assessment before proceeding. This article cannot determine what is happening in a particular attic, and moisture response depends on the assembly and the circumstances, not just the insulation label.

## Air sealing is a separate part of the job

Loose-fill insulation is not a substitute for air sealing. Air can move through gaps around attic-floor penetrations, and insulation alone does not reliably close those openings. Ask whether air sealing is included in the quote, what areas it covers, and whether the contractor will identify any conditions that need attention before adding insulation.

The Department of Energy’s [air-sealing guidance for existing attics](https://bsesc.energy.gov/energy-basics/air-sealing-existing-attics) treats air sealing as a distinct step. Compare bids carefully: one may include sealing work while another prices insulation only. If the scopes differ, the totals are not an apples-to-apples comparison.

Do not attempt work around electrical components, suspect asbestos, mold, combustion equipment, or spray-foam chemicals as a do-it-yourself project. Have a qualified professional evaluate safety concerns.

## A practical way to compare bids

Use a short checklist to keep the comparison focused:

- **Material and product:** Is the exact insulation product named?
- **Preparation:** Does the bid include inspection, air sealing, or removal where needed?
- **Coverage:** Are the areas and installation approach clearly described?
- **Existing conditions:** Does the plan address moisture, ventilation, and existing insulation?
- **Verification:** How will the installer check and document completed work?
- **Scope differences:** Are you comparing the same work across both proposals?

If a contractor recommends one material, ask why it fits your attic’s conditions and request product-specific documentation. If a proposal makes a broad claim about moisture, settling, or air sealing, ask what evidence applies to the product and assembly being proposed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is cellulose or fiberglass always better for blown-in insulation?**

No single material is best for every attic. Compare the exact product, installation plan, existing conditions, and the full scope of each quote.

**Does blown-in insulation seal attic air leaks?**

Do not assume that it does. Ask whether air sealing is included as a separate part of the work and what the contractor plans to address.

**What should I do if my attic insulation is wet?**

Ask a qualified professional to investigate the source of moisture and assess the attic before new insulation is added. Insulation does not correct a leak or resolve the cause of dampness.
